pages.text: $(bold)Description:$() Five OBSR specifications are available in the field, all differentiated from the same prototype. Their functions are distinct.
pages.title: Model Overview

pages.text: $(li)$(bold)OBSR-2 - Semantic Lock$(): protects recorded targets.$(br)$(li)$(bold)OBSR-1 - Guided Mutation$(): changes where a drift within range goes.$(br)$(li)$(bold)OBSR-Health - Bio Stabiliser$(): runs on creatures within range to stabilise every block and creature there.

$(li)$(bold)OBSR-EX - Total Stability$(): the complete classifier of the previous iteration. Fixed coverage, unaffected by stage decay.$(br)$(li)$(bold)OBSR-3 - Candidate Observer$(): not used as a stabilisation device.
pages.title: Model Overview (cont.)

pages.text: $(bold)Stage decay:$() The intensification of defocus erodes the effectiveness of stabilisation devices.$(br2)$(li)OBSR-2's lock becomes probabilistic in the final stage;$(br)$(li)OBSR-1's completeness is halved in the final stage.
OBSR-Health and OBSR-EX are unaffected by stage decay.$(br2)The effects of multiple bases do not stack; the nearest one is used.

$(bold)Copying loss:$() The parameters of OBSR-EX are hard-wired. Copying it is recasting: every recasting loses classification precision, and its coverage shrinks with it.$(br2)There is a generation cap on recasting.
A Candidate Observer built around a copy requires more training, the more so at higher generations.$(br2)There is only one original. Use it with care.
